hoover.headline: An archive in the sky
hoover.body: Arthur Brown Jr. gave Hoover's peace archive a 285-foot landmark, with stucco tinted to echo the Main Quad's sandstone.

hoover.headline: The bells crossed oceans
hoover.body: The carillon began with 35 bells from Belgium's World's Fair pavilion. It now holds 48; the largest calls for peace.

hoover.headline: Hear it above the campus
hoover.body: The carillon shares the tower's 14th floor with an observation deck. Look out where the sound travels.

hoover.headline: A secret on the ground floor
hoover.body: During World War II, a radio room here monitored foreign military broadcasts and relayed news.

huang.headline: The gift behind the gateway
huang.body: Jensen Huang earned a Stanford engineering master's. He and Lori gave $30 million to build this engineering anchor.

huang.headline: A hub for what comes next
huang.body: The dean's office, Terman Library, and 300-seat NVIDIA Auditorium share this engineering crossroads.

huang.headline: The web in toy blocks
huang.body: Page and Brin's original PageRank test servers sit in the lobby, wrapped in colorful toy building blocks.

huang.headline: A quieter kind of power
huang.body: Huang anchors the east–west engineering quad while using about half the energy of a comparable building.

mainquad.headline: The campus began here
mainquad.body: Olmsted planned the grounds; Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge designed the Quad that opened with Stanford.

mainquad.headline: The axis was a choice
mainquad.body: Olmsted imagined a foothill campus and an off-center church. Leland Stanford chose the flat site and centered it.

mainquad.headline: The arch became a ghost
mainquad.body: The earthquake took down the grand Memorial Arch. Its bases still mark the entrance where the arch once stood.

mainquad.headline: A message under your feet
mainquad.body: Seniors lay a plaque and bury a time capsule along the Inner Quad arcade. New stories enter the old stones.

hpgarage.headline: Birthplace of Silicon Valley
hpgarage.body: Encouraged by professor Frederick Terman, Bill Hewlett and David Packard started HP in this garage. It's California Historical Landmark 976.

memchu.headline: Jane's memorial in mosaic
memchu.body: Jane Stanford built it for Leland as a church for all faiths. The facade mosaic out front is 84 feet wide and 30 feet high.

varian.headline: A lab named for an inventor
varian.body: Gardner Dailey designed it for Physics and the Hansen Experimental Physics Lab. Its namesake's big idea came earlier: the klystron.

spilker.headline: Named for a GPS pioneer
spilker.body: James Spilker Jr. designed the civilian GPS signal, part of how this map knows where you are. He and Anna Marie pledged $31 million toward it.

moore.headline: A gift from Intel's founder
moore.body: Gordon and Betty Moore made the naming gift. Moore wasn't a Stanford graduate, yet he gave to Stanford for about four decades.

gates.headline: Where Google got its start
gates.body: Larry Page and Sergey Brin developed PageRank here. An IEEE Milestone plaque on the fourth floor marks the birth of Google.

packard.headline: A record gift, built in glass
packard.body: David Packard and Bill Hewlett gave $77.4 million to rebuild this corner of campus. Its glass prow lets passersby see engineering at work.

y2e2.headline: A building that breathes
y2e2.body: Its windows open and close on their own with the temperature and wind, and it uses about 57 percent less energy than a typical building.

shriram.headline: The quad's largest building
shriram.body: Bioengineering and Chemical Engineering share 34 specialized labs here, in a building using about half the power of a typical one.

allen.headline: A guitar at the dedication
allen.body: It opened as the Center for Integrated Systems and took the Paul G. Allen Foundation's name. Paul Allen played electric guitar at its 1997 dedication.

hewlett.headline: A record pledge
hewlett.body: Bill Hewlett's $50 million pledge was Stanford's largest from one person at the time. With Packard, it marks the engineering quad's entrance.

cantor.headline: A museum for their son
cantor.body: It opened as the Leland Stanford Junior Museum, the Stanfords' memorial to their only child. Outside, the Rodin garden holds 20 bronzes.

mccullough.headline: Built for materials science
mccullough.body: A $1.5 million grant from vacuum tube pioneer Jack McCullough, his wife, and DARPA paid for it. Varian's architect, Gardner Dailey, designed it.

durand.headline: Named for a propeller pioneer
durand.body: Professor William F. Durand's research led to the first variable pitch propeller. His building is home to Aeronautics and Astronautics.

sequoia.headline: Home of Statistics
sequoia.body: The new Sequoia Hall, with its Girshick library, was dedicated with remarks from President Gerhard Casper and Provost Condoleezza Rice.

greenearth.headline: A gift from TI's co-founder
greenearth.body: Cecil Green co-founded Texas Instruments. He never attended Stanford, but he and Ida helped fund this Earth Sciences research building.

mitchell.headline: A library on the second floor
mitchell.body: The Ruth Wattis Mitchell Earth Sciences Building houses Earth Sciences departments and the Branner Earth Sciences Library.

gilbert.headline: Named for a zoologist
gilbert.body: The Charles H. Gilbert Biological Sciences Building houses the Biology department. Gilbert's own story starts in a high school classroom.

clark.headline: Three wings around a courtyard
clark.body: Jim Clark of Silicon Graphics and Netscape made a $90 million lead gift. Foster and Partners designed this home of Bio-X.

likashing.headline: Where doctors learn by doing
likashing.body: The medical school's teaching hub holds a 28,000 square foot center for simulation and immersive learning on its ground floor.

coda.headline: Built in binary
coda.body: CoDa's two wings, one rectangular and one oval, stand for the ones and zeros of binary code. It houses Computer Science, Statistics and Data Science.

bassbio.headline: Biology under one roof
bassbio.body: Its 133,000 square feet of wet and dry labs brought the Biology department together from five aging buildings.

sapp.headline: Thirty years behind a fence
sapp.body: Old Chem sat fenced off for almost 30 years after the 1989 earthquake. Restored for science teaching, it now carries the Sapp family's name.

oldunion.headline: Stanford's first student union
oldunion.body: Its three buildings began as women's dorms and the first union. Bakewell and Brown, Green Library's architects, gave it a Spanish Colonial look.

tresidder.headline: Built around the oaks
tresidder.body: Architect Bill Busse gave the union a meandering shape to fit around four huge oak trees. Only two of them survive.

greenlib.headline: Paid for with jewels
greenlib.body: Jane Stanford directed $500,000 from the sale of her jewels to the library. This wing opened with room for more than 700,000 books.

lathrop.headline: A library with a past life
lathrop.body: The business school's former South Building became the undergraduate library, with a 24-hour study space and a digital language lab.

bookstore.headline: The corner students meet
bookstore.body: The Bookstore has stood in White Plaza since 1960. The plaza and the Claw fountain beside it were both built in 1964.

littlefield.headline: Faculty under one roof
littlefield.body: Edmund Littlefield's lead gift of about $5 million built this Kohn Pedersen Fox design, which held offices for most of the business school's faculty.
